scenes.title: dbt Macros & Jinja
scenes.narration: This lesson introduces Jinja templating and macros, the tools dbt gives you to write reusable, dynamic SQL.

scenes.title: Jinja is the templating layer
bullets: Everything in double braces is Jinja, not SQL
ref and source are themselves Jinja functions
dbt compiles Jinja into plain SQL before running
scenes.narration: Jinja is the templating language woven through every dbt project. Anything you see inside double curly braces is Jinja rather than raw SQL, and in fact the ref and source functions you already use are Jinja calls. dbt renders all of this templating into plain SQL during compilation, so the warehouse only ever sees ordinary queries.

scenes.title: What macros are for
bullets: Reusable snippets of SQL logic, like functions
Defined once and called from many models
scenes.narration: A macro is essentially a function that returns a piece of SQL. You define a repeated pattern once and then call it from as many models as you like, which eliminates copy-paste and gives you a single place to change the logic. Macros are how teams keep large dbt projects consistent and maintainable.

scenes.title: Defining and calling a macro
scenes.narration: This macro converts a cents column into dollars. We define it once with a parameter for the column name, and inside it returns the rounding expression. In a model we call the macro and pass the actual column, and at compile time dbt substitutes the expression directly into the SQL. If the rounding rule ever changes, you edit the macro alone and every model that calls it updates automatically.

scenes.title: Control flow with Jinja
scenes.narration: Jinja also brings loops and conditionals to your SQL. Here a for loop generates one conditional count column per status value, and the loop.last check adds a comma between columns but not after the final one. Instead of hand-writing repetitive columns, you describe the pattern once and let Jinja expand it. This is how you keep wide, repetitive queries dry and easy to extend.

scenes.text: Use dbt compile to inspect the rendered SQL, and keep macros focused so your models stay readable rather than over-templated.
scenes.narration: A good guardrail is to use dbt compile to inspect the SQL your Jinja actually produces, and to keep macros small and focused so your models stay readable rather than turning into an unreadable maze of templating.
